title: Adaptive lane sheriff prioritizer for plan tiers
creator: Sofia Martinez
description:
Summary: Implement an admission and prioritization component (internal name: 'lane-sheriff') that enforces plan-tier policies (free, paid, enterprise) while doing quota-aware admission and graceful fallback to compatible model variants and regions. This ticket covers design, implementation, and rollout of the prioritizer that sits in front of the request router and the admission controller.

Background: Current tier routing is rule-based and often results in noisy failures when a tier hits its daily or burst quota. We need a smarter policy that: balances latency SLOs, preserves enterprise tenant guarantees, allows paid customers to get preferential admission during pressure, and offers best-effort degraded paths for free users (e.g., lower-capacity model variant or increased sampling latency). The lane-sheriff should integrate with quota metadata, token-estimate heuristics, regional capacity signals, and model-variant compatibility matrix.

Goals:
- Reduce customer-facing 429s for paid/enterprise customers by >50% during high load events.
- Keep median tail latency for enterprise routes within SLOs by prioritizing admission and routing to healthy regions/model variants.
- Provide deterministic, auditable fallback decisions (which variant chosen, why, and which policy applied).
- Ensure free tier gets a predictable degraded experience rather than opaque errors.

Scope:
- Admission logic and prioritizer service + config schema.
- Integrations: quota service (read-only), routing control plane, model-variant catalog, regional capacity signals.
- Metrics, instrumentation, and dashboard surfaces.
- Canary rollout and rollback plan.

Out of scope: billing changes, quota charging semantics, or UI console features beyond basic observability links.
acceptance_criteria: A deterministic prioritizer component is implemented and deployed to staging behind feature flag
Paid and enterprise routes observe >50% reduction in quota-related rejects in staging ingress under synthetic high-load test
Fallbacks to lower-cost model variants occur with annotated trace metadata (policy id, reason, selected variant)
Audit logs contain admission decision, estimated token cost, region chosen, and final routed model variant for every fallback event
End-to-end latency regression for enterprise routes is within +5% of baseline under normal load
Feature flag allows immediate disable and full rollback with no config changes to core router
design_notes:
Core idea: a lightweight prioritizer service evaluates each incoming request and returns an admission verdict plus a routing hint. The decision uses: (1) plan tier weight (enterprise>paid>free), (2) quota headroom from quota service (soft quota estimate + burst allowance), (3) predicted token cost based on prompt heuristics, (4) region health score (capacity, latency, active-util), (5) model-variant compatibility and cost profile. We will expose policy rules as ordered predicates that can be tuned without deploy (config map) and include per-tenant overrides.

Admission outcomes: admit with primary route, admit with degraded route (lower-capacity variant or batch-friendly path), defer (queue with short backoff), or reject with recommended action. Degraded routes must be labeled so consumers and the Console can attribute quality regressions.

Safety: avoid oscillation via token-window smoothing and request-sampling feedback. Use reservoir counters per-tier and region with exponential decay to approximate headroom. The service should be stateless for scaling; counters live in a high-throughput time-series store (short TTL).
implementation_plan:
1) Spec the policy schema and small DSL for predicates; land config proto.
2) Build lightweight prioritizer service (Go) with read-only adapters to quota API, regional telemetry, and variant catalog.
3) Implement token estimate heuristic in SDK quick path and server fallback (server estimates when missing).
4) Add tracing headers and audit log emitters.
5) Wire prioritizer into the router as a pre-admit hook behind FF.
6) Add feature-flagging and rollout gates (canary by customer ID and region).
7) Create synthetic load harness to validate behavior under overloaded scenarios.
8) Iterate on tuning rules for burst windows and smoothing.

Milestones: design spec -> infra PRs -> prioritizer service -> router integration -> staging canary -> prod rollout.
rollout_plan:
Phase 1 (staging): enable FF for internal test accounts and run synthetic stress tests that simulate mixed-tier traffic. Validate metrics.
Phase 2 (canary): enable FF for 5% of traffic (mix of paid and free tenants) in us-west-2 for a 48h window. Monitor reject rate, enterprise latency, and error budgets.
Phase 3 (regional ramp): expand to us-east-1 and eu-west-1 with 25% traffic and additional monitoring.
Phase 4 (global): enable for all regions and gradually increase config aggressiveness for free-tier degradations.
Rollback: FF toggle to off + flush in-progress queued requests; monitor for SLO regressions for 30 minutes post-rollback.
test_plan: Unit tests for policy evaluation and predicate DSL. Integration tests that mock quota and region signals to assert correct admission decisions. End-to-end chaos test that grills regional capacity and confirms fallbacks pick compatible model variants. Synthetic load test scenarios: bursty short-duration spikes, sustained high throughput, and adversarial small-token high-QPS patterns. Add golden trace tests to ensure audit log format stability.
metrics:
Emit metrics per decision: prioritize.admit{tier,region,variant}, prioritize.degrade{from_variant,to_variant}, prioritize.defer, prioritize.reject; histogram for decision_latency_ms; gauges for estimated_headroom per tier-region; counter for audit_log_emitted. Alert rules: paid_reject_rate > 0.5% for 10m, enterprise_latency_percentile95 > SLO by 10% for 5m.
Success metrics: reduce paid/enterprise quota rejects by >50% during synthetic overload; maintain enterprise p95 latency within SLO in canary window.
